Building on the first ALMA technosignature survey (Mason et al. 2025), we identify four searches ALMA2040 is uniquely placed to make: (i) narrowband searches using a phased-up, beamformed array, extending the commensal model pioneered for the VLA and MeerKAT into a regime where drift rates reach ~ 103 Hz s^-1; (ii) broadband aggregate leakage (BRaTs) from Kardashev Type I civilisations, for which 128-512 GHz of instantaneous bandwidth places a ~ 60 pc horizon within an integration time of one hour on source; (iii) Dysonian searches for the cold waste heat of computation - Slysh haloes - whose arcsecond and subarcsecond angular scales around M dwarfs are well matched to ALMA2040's array configuration; and (iv) geometric discontinuities imprinted by occulting megastructures, detectable as ringing in the visibility function with a phased ALMA operating in a mm/sub-mm VLBI array. We set out the corresponding requirements: bandwidth, beamforming, commensal access, spectral resolution and sub-second time resolution.

papers.title: Chemical Demographics of Star-forming Regions
papers.abstract: Our understanding of complex organic chemistry during the formation of stars and planets is shaped by a handful of cherry-picked sources with bright molecular emission lines. This observational bias impedes our assessment of how universal chemical complexity is during star formation. The lack of systematic wideband spectral surveys for statistically significant samples of protostars and cores is a major roadblock to properly probing how COM inventories and abundances depend on the vast range of physical conditions, local cloud and global galactic environments, and evolutionary timescales of low- and high-mass star formation. In turn, this limits our ability to constrain and test physicochemical models, which depend critically on these parameters. The next-generation ALMA2040, with a 10x improvement in line sensitivity, is required to observe COMs, that we perceive as common today, in a fraction of the observing time that is needed today with ALMA. Such capabilities will propel us into the era of chemical demographics, whereby wideband (>100 GHz) spectral surveys at high sensitivity (routinely probing COM abundances down to 0.01% relative to CH3OH) will be executed towards >1000-10000 prestellar and protostellar sources. With robust chemical inventories towards large source sample sizes, we will be able to probe for dependencies of chemical complexity on mass regime, feedback processes in a cluster, Galactic position, metallicity, and time-variable accretion. Only with statistically significant samples at high sensitivity will we be able to assess the ubiquity and homogeneity of COM chemistry across the protostellar mass spectrum and natal cores. Constraining the diversity and availability of such species is critical for our understanding of the chemical reservoir available for planet formation, which eventually shapes (exo)planetary atmosphere compositions.

papers.title: A Search for Dust in the Outflow of the HH212 Class 0 Protostellar System
papers.abstract: Perhaps the most visually striking phenomenon during star formation is the ejection of material along the direction of the protostar's rotational axis. Observed in the form of molecular outflows and/or atomic jets, these features carry away mass, energy and angular momentum from the system. Given the known dust content of protoplanetary disks, and the energetics of outflows, it has been suggested that it should be possible to lift dust from disks via winds, yet limited observational evidence has been presented in the literature. Any detection of dust within protostellar outflows not only puts constraints on the dust content in outflows, but if a sufficient amount of dust can be removed from the system, the mass budget for planet formation could also be affected. We present re-imaging of archival, multi-frequency dust continuum observations taken with the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array (ALMA) towards the HH212 protostellar system. We detect an extension in the dust emission, and using multi-frequency data in Bands 7 and 9, we estimate the spectral index of the emitting dust and the dust mass in the wind launching region. We find a small but still significant amount of dust mass coincident with the molecular outflow cavity. This finding is assessed in relation to the hypothesis that the outflow could be capable of transporting dust away from the HH212 protoplanetary disk.

papers.title: Beyond Mergers: the Role of Metallicity in Forming a Reservoir of Massive and Detached Binary Black Hole Systems
papers.abstract: Isolated binary evolution is a key pathway to forming binary black hole (BBH) mergers. However, the observed gravitational-wave population indicates it may not account for all mergers, especially those with high primary black hole mass ($\gtrsim 30 M_{\odot}$). Using the binary population synthesis code \texttt{POSYDON}, we simulate populations of binary systems at eight metallicities from $10^{-4}$ to $2\,Z_\odot$ and classify each BH-forming binary as a merging BBH, a detached BBH, or a system disrupted during BH formation. We find that metallicity shapes these populations differently, especially for high BH masses ($\gtrsim 25 M_{\odot}$). At lower metallicities, between $10^{-2}$ and $0.45\,Z_\odot$, massive BHs continue to form but become increasingly unlikely to merge: the number of massive merging BBHs declines sharply, while the detached population remains abundant. For $25$--$35\,M_\odot$ BHs, the detached-to-merging ratio increases by more than two orders of magnitude across this metallicity range. After weighting by cosmic star formation, massive BHs are found predominantly in detached binaries with orbital periods $\gtrsim 10^2$ days. Therefore, isolated binary evolution can form massive BBHs even if it rarely produces massive BBH mergers, leaving behind a massive and detached population that may be driven to merger through dynamical interactions in dense stellar environments.

papers.title: EPRV Asteroseismology of the K dwarfs GJ 570 A and GJ 783 A with ESPRESSO. Empirical mode-amplitude scaling in tension with 3D convection simulations
authors: M. J. P. F. G. Monteiro
papers.abstract: Solar-like oscillations in K dwarfs have intrinsically low amplitudes, making them challenging to detect in space-based photometry. The advent of Extremely Precise Radial Velocity (EPRV) instrumentation enables Doppler asteroseismology in the mid-K regime, providing a new opportunity to test mode-excitation and damping physics. We investigate the scaling of oscillation amplitudes with stellar parameters and assess whether 3D surface convection simulations reproduce the observed amplitude behavior. High-cadence ESPRESSO radial-velocity time series were obtained over five and six consecutive nights for the K dwarfs GJ 570 A (K4 V) and GJ 783 A (K2.5 V), respectively. We identified oscillation modes from weighted power spectra and extracted them via sine-wave fitting following spectral deconvolution. Peak mode amplitudes were measured from heavily smoothed power spectra. For comparison, we performed 3D radiative-hydrodynamical simulations including excitation and damping-rate calculations. We measured 6 modes for GJ 570 A and 24 for GJ 783 A ($\ell=0$-$2$, and $\ell=3$ for GJ 783 A). The peak radial-mode amplitudes are $2.57 \pm 0.52\:{\rm cm\,s^{-1}}$ and $4.90 \pm 0.81\:{\rm cm\,s^{-1}}$, respectively. These results support a transition from an $\sim(L/M)^{0.7}$ amplitude scaling to a steeper $\sim(L/M)^{1.5}$ scaling, occurring near the G/K-dwarf boundary toward decreasing $L/M$. In contrast, 3D simulations predict an $\sim(L/M)^{0.9}$ scaling for K dwarfs, revealing tension between observations and first-principles convection models. EPRV asteroseismology extends into the mid-K regime and exposes a steep mode-amplitude scaling that our 3D convection simulations do not reproduce. This discrepancy points to missing physics in our implementation of convection-pulsation coupling and/or limitations in the adopted modeling assumptions, motivating further theoretical investigation.

papers.title: Finite-Element Asteroseismology I: Two-Dimensional Adiabatic Oscillations of Rapidly Rotating N=3 Polytropes
papers.abstract: We develop a finite-element formulation for linear adiabatic oscillations of axisymmetric uniformly rotating, centrifugally distorted, self-gravitating N=3 polytropes. Equilibrium models are constructed using self-consistent-field iteration and then remeshed on a surface-fitted oblate meridional domain. The quadratic eigenvalue problem describing oscillations for each azimuthal wavenumber $m$ is solved using a conforming two-domain mesh. The density-weighted displacement, $\boldsymbol{u}=\rho^{1/2}\boldsymbol{\xi}$, is defined in the stellar interior, whereas the gravitational-potential perturbation $\delta\Phi$ is solved both inside the star and in an exterior vacuum. The coupled displacement--potential problem is assembled and solved within FEniCSx as a polynomial eigenvalue problem. Without rotation, the axisymmetric modes agree closely with an independent one-dimensional calculation. For finite rotation rates, several clean axisymmetric $p$-mode branches of the spheroidal star successfully reproduce the frequencies tabulated by Reese (2006). The relative frequency differences induced by rotation are smaller than $3\times10^{-4}$ for the low-order mode branches up to $\sim 60$\% of the critical rotation rate. These tests validate both the centrifugally distorted equilibrium and the finite-element implementation. We develop a method to track eigenfunctions continuously as a function of rotation and decompose their angular structure to quantify rotational mode mixing and progressive coupling between different spherical harmonic components. This reveals continuous deformation of individual mode branches from nearly single-$\ell$ structures to strongly mixed states at rapid rotation. This work is intended as a step toward finite-element multidimensional asteroseismology frameworks for modelling realistic rotationally and tidally distorted stellar configurations.

papers.title: An HST survey of photometry and multiplicity of brown dwarfs and planetary-mass objects in the field of Taurus
papers.abstract: We present a photometric and multiplicity survey of 26 young objects with masses between 6 Mj and 37 Mj and spectral type later than M8 in the Taurus star-forming region with the Hubble Space Telescope. We search for companion candidates using two methods: a dedicated photometric technique based on the combination of colours from multi-band photometry and point spread function fitting. No companion candidates are detected beyond 30 au. With an updated membership and age identification, we determine luminosity, temperature, and mass for the 26 young objects using evolutionary models. We demonstrate that our HST observations are sensitive to companions down to masses of 1 Mj and even lower for some targets by artificial star injection tests. After survey completeness correction, we derive a binary frequency < 6.5% for this sample in the 68% confidence interval for companions with mass ratios between 0.1 and 1 and separations between 30 and 7,000 au. We find no significant difference in binary frequency among planetary-mass objects in Taurus, Upper Scorpius, and the field. These findings support that the binary frequency of planetary-mass objects is settled at young ages, probably younger than 1--10 Myr, suggesting that the formation of wide-orbit planetary-mass binaries is inefficient and the disruption of them likely occurs at a very early stage in a low density environment.

papers.title: Influence of numerical domain design in simulations of solar coronal heating with the MAGEC code
papers.abstract: Numerical simulations are essential for studying the solar atmosphere, especially in the context of the coronal heating problem. Understanding how numerical factors and boundary conditions (BC) influence the energetic structure of these models is crucial for unraveling coronal heating mechanisms. We investigate how the computational domain dimensions, upper BC, and vertical grid resolution influence the relaxed thermal structure, energetics, and long-term stability of 2D solar atmosphere simulations with a vertical magnetic field. Using the MAGEC code, we conducted parametric studies varying domain width and height, vertical grid stretching, and top BC, including hot-plate, closed, unrestricted temperature, background heating, and non-reflecting characteristic configurations. We evaluated average temperature profiles for parameter dependence and temporal stability, and analyzed the energetic budget as a function of height, isolating contributions from radiative losses, thermal conduction, pressure work, and internal energy flux. Models with larger vertical domains show higher average coronal temperatures and steeper transition region gradients. Among the less artificial BC, non-reflecting characteristics most effectively delay coronal cooling. We determined the threshold height at which a dynamic top BC can mimic fixed-temperature setups, and established the maximum allowable grid stretching that preserves physical accuracy while reducing computational costs. The energetic terms change significantly with the chosen BC, with specific mechanisms acting as cooling agents in different atmospheric layers. Our results demonstrate that domain height, vertical grid design, and BC critically dictate the relaxed thermal structure and energetic balance of the simulated solar atmosphere.

papers.title: Investigation of an X-class Flare and Quasi-Periodic Pulsations in NOAA AR 13842 using SDO, Aditya-L1 and Solar Orbiter
papers.abstract: We investigate an X9.0 class flare (SOL2024-10-03T12:08) and associated quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) in NOAA active region (AR) 13842 using observations from the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), Aditya-L1 and Solar Orbiter (SO). To explore the role of magnetic configuration in the flare, we employ non-force-free-field extrapolation technique for reconstructing a sequence of the coronal magnetic field throughout the flare. The observations reveal the emergence of intricate flare brightenings and ribbons. QPPs are observed with periods of $\approx$ 2 and $\approx$ 6 minutes in EUV, $\approx$ 7 minutes in UV, and $\approx$ 1 minute in X-rays. The extrapolation documents the presence of a flux rope, a sheared arcade, and a hyperbolic flux tube (HFT) enveloping the rope and the arcade. The sequence of the extrapolation illustrates an increase in the twist of the rope as it ascends towards a torus-unstable region, thereby rendering the rope a viable candidate for eruption. The sheared arcade appears to generate electric current through its foot-point's motion, which explains the sigmoidal brightening observed at the flare onset. The motion also seems to drive the non-parallel field lines closer together, heightening gradient in the magnetic field beneath the rope. Consequently, recurrent magnetic reconnection is anticipated within the sheared arcade --- explaining the ascent of the rope with its twist increment. The formation of parallel flare ribbons is attributed to these reconnections. Furthermore, reconnection at the HFT is proposed to lead the remote and quasi-circular ribbons. Crucially, repeated reconnections inside the arcade as well as at the HFT are speculated to cause the QPPs.

papers.title: Orbital Stability of Apsidally Aligned Planetary Systems
papers.abstract: The dynamical stability of compact planetary systems is known to depend strongly on orbital eccentricities, but the physical role of apsidal alignment remains poorly understood. We investigate this problem using direct {\em N}-body simulations by separating planetary eccentricities into a systematic component shared by all planets and a random component that determines the degree of apsidal alignment. We find that these two components play fundamentally different dynamical roles. Random eccentricity destabilizes planetary systems by driving neighboring planet pairs into the regime of mean-motion resonance overlap, leading to chaotic evolution. In contrast, systematic eccentricity has little effect on the instability timescale over a wide range of values because the planetary orbits remain in apsidal alignment, preserving nearly fixed relative orbital orientations despite finite eccentricities. As a result, systems that start in apsidal alignment are nearly as stable as initially circular systems. This protection mechanism has a finite domain of validity. Beyond a critical systematic eccentricity, coherent apsidal precession breaks down, differential precession develops, and the instability timescale decreases rapidly. Our results demonstrate that the long-term stability of compact planetary systems cannot be characterized solely by orbital eccentricities but also depends on the maintenance of coherent apsidal precession, providing a new direction for analytical stability criteria.

papers.title: Dust Activity Evolution and Constraints on Icy Grains in the Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS
papers.abstract: We present Zwicky Transient Facility observations of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS to characterize its dust-activity evolution before and after perihelion. Before perihelion, the effective scattering cross section $C_{\rm e}$ brightened across the inner $2\times10^4$ km as $C_{\rm e}\propto r_{\rm H}^{-\gamma}$, with $\gamma$ increasing from $1.63\pm0.14$ to $1.88\pm0.34$ with aperture size. After perihelion, the heliocentric index decreased from $2.44\pm0.09$ in the $5\times10^3$ km aperture to $1.54\pm0.09$ in the $8\times10^4$ km aperture, indicating faster fading of the inner coma. Under adopted grain-size and residence-time assumptions, the implied dust mass-loss rates are $\sim123$--$203~{\rm kg~s^{-1}}$ before perihelion and $\sim596$--$1412~{\rm kg~s^{-1}}$ after perihelion. The morphology yields a sunward ejection-speed scale of $v_{\rm ej}\sim(190\pm3)a_{\mu{\rm m}}^{-1/2}~{\rm m~s^{-1}}$ and an effective perpendicular velocity of $v_\perp=(79\pm6)a_{\mu{\rm m}}^{-1/2}~{\rm m~s^{-1}}$. Post-perihelion surface-brightness profiles transiently steepened to $k\sim-2.7$ in late November and early December, then became shallower and approached $k=-1.5$ by January. Matched $g-r$ profiles show that this phase coincided with an anomalously blue outer coma that disappeared by January. We characterize the fading component with a projected destruction length of $\ell_{\rm DE}\sim(6.4$--$7.2)\times10^4$ km. Thermophysical sublimation calculations indicate that this scale, together with the order of magnitude of the water production near the main imaging epoch, is consistent with $a_0\sim5$--$10~\mu{\rm m}$ icy grains containing a small absorbing carbonaceous fraction of $f_{\rm C}\sim0.1\%$. These results suggest that the early post-perihelion coma likely contained a short-lived, volatile-bearing icy-grain component whose fading contributed to the outer-coma brightness and color evolution

papers.title: Post-perihelion dust activity and a candidate icy-grain halo in long-period comet C/2023 A3 (Tsuchinshan--ATLAS)
papers.abstract: We analyze the post-perihelion coma of the Great Comet of 2024, C/2023 A3 (Tsuchinshan--ATLAS) to characterize dust activity and assess the contribution of sublimating icy grains to a candidate near-nucleus halo. Using archival Zwicky Transient Facility images from 15 February to 26 May 2025, we performed aperture photometry within a fixed projected radius of 40,000 km and derived azimuthally averaged surface-brightness profiles. The comet faded from 12.86 to 14.77 mag as heliocentric distance increased from 2.64 to 3.90 au, with two short-lived brightenings. The effective dust cross section decreased by a factor of 2.4, following $C_{\rm e}\propto r_{\rm h}^{-3.1}$, while the dust mass production rate scaled as $\dot{M}_{\rm d}\propto r_{\rm h}^{-3.41}$, consistent with a contribution from water-ice-driven activity. Extrapolating the fitted relation to perihelion implies a model-dependent cumulative dust mass loss of $3.0\times10^{11}$ kg, equivalent to a globally averaged erosion depth of $\sim1.4$ m for an assumed nucleus radius of 5.9 km. Coma profiles were shallower than the canonical steady-state expectation, suggesting radial changes in dust distribution or scattering properties, possibly due to delayed aggregate fragmentation. A persistent central brightness excess, coincident with less-red inner-coma colors, is consistent with an icy-grain halo. Among the models explored, icy grains of radius $\sim10~\mu$m with carbon fraction $\sim0.1\%$ yield halo radii comparable to those observed during enhanced activity on 21--25 February 2025, with grain lifetimes of $2.8\times10^5$--$3.2\times10^5$ s. No single fixed grain size and composition reproduces the full halo evolution; an increasing carbon fraction could explain the broad halo-radius trend, possibly reflecting progressive refractory enrichment of near-surface material.

papers.title: Thermodynamics of Viscously Heated Circumplanetary Disks
papers.abstract: Circumplanetary disks (CPDs) play an important role in the formation of gas giants and their satellites, yet remain poorly understood owing to the lack of observables and comprehensive theoretical models. Incorporating $\alpha$-viscosity, a free-fall prescription of mass infall and boundary layer accretion, we develop an axisymmetric viscous radiation hydrodynamic (RHD) model. We evolve this model for different physical parameters using the RHD code {\tt Guangqi}, which solves RHD equations under the flux-limited diffusion approximation. In eight out of nine simulations, we obtain quasi-steady-state solutions and verify self-consistent energy conversion and transport. Overall, disk thickness increases with accretion rate and decreases with planet mass, consistent with the expected trend in conventional $\alpha$-disk models. On the other hand, we highlight that the boundary layer plays a significant role in setting angular momentum transport and thermodynamics of the inner CPD, yielding ``hot'' ($s_{\rm real}>11\,k_{\rm{B}}\,m_{\rm{H}}^{-1}$) accreted gas, and potentially leading to dust sublimation. We identify a supersonic accretion flow, amounting to $2\%$--$5\%$ of the total accretion rate, located at high elevations above the CPDs with low angular momentum in our simulations. If the planet is massive ($\gtrsim3\,M_{\rm J}$), this low angular momentum flow impacting the planetary surface could generate observable H$\alpha$ emission when the shock accretion rate is $\gtrsim5.5\times10^{-8}\, M_{\rm J}\,\rm{yr}^{-1}$.

papers.title: A first look at the protoplanet WISPIT 2 b with VLTI/GRAVITY+
papers.abstract: Confirmed observations of young protoplanets actively undergoing the process of formation have remained rare to date. In this Letter, we present new insights into the nature of the recently identified protoplanet WISPIT 2 b (age $\sim$ 5 Myr) from VLTI/GRAVITY+ observations. Through the analysis of the spectral energy distribution (SED) and astrometry of WISPIT 2 b, with the inclusion of new GRAVITY+ data, we investigate the nature of the protoplanet's thermal emission and orbital properties. We performed an orbit fit with the inclusion of new high-precision GRAVITY+ astrometry to provide an updated orbital solution. We also analyzed the medium resolution GRAVITY+ K band spectrum in combination with new VLT/SPHERE and literature photometry, exploring both the atmospheric properties and the constraints on the circumplanetary environment. Finally, we checked for any signal from a resolved circumplanetary disk in the GRAVITY+ data. We detected the protoplanet WISPIT 2 b at $\sim$322 mas separation from its host star. The new GRAVITY+ astrometry prefers an orbit with a moderate eccentricity. Analysis of the SED reveals an effective temperature in the 900 to 1300 K regime and a slight preference for atmospheric models including clouds over pure blackbody emission. While the GRAVITY+ observations do also not resolve a circumplanetary disk, we place an upper limit on the possible spatial extent of such a disk. The new GRAVITY+ observations independently confirm WISPIT 2 b as a self-luminous and point-like companion residing inside the gap of the transitional disk at $\sim$60 au from its host star. Further observations - either at higher signal-to-noise ratio or at longer wavelengths - are required to characterize the atmosphere and examine the presence of circumplanetary material from thermal emission of the dust.

papers.title: LSST and Keck characterization of outer Main Belt comet P/2026 N2
papers.abstract: We characterize comet P/2026 N2, whose outer Main Belt orbit has $a=3.07$ au, $e=0.21$, and $i=2.25^\circ$, using optical observations, archival imaging, and dynamical integrations. Observations from the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) at NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory in 2026 June-July and Keck/LRIS imaging on October 7 show active morphology across perihelion over 102 days. Within a projected aperture radius of approximately 1,000 km, Keck colors of $g-r=0.50\pm0.05$ and $r-i=0.06\pm0.06$ mag are consistent with nearly neutral B/C-complex reflectance. Phase-corrected $a(0^\circ)f\rho=3.66\pm0.12$ cm in derived $r$ and $3.46\pm0.17$ cm in $i$ are comparable to LSST measurements. The geometry-corrected $i$-band aperture brightness changes by $0.07\pm0.07$ mag between July 9 and October 7; the 2,000 km $r$-band aperture measurements are also consistent between epochs. These results support sustained observable activity, consistent with prolonged or recurrent dust production. Archival DECam images recover N2 on 2021 July 4, but its activity state is inconclusive. A 5,000-particle forward integration retains a concentrated outer Main Belt core throughout 50 Myr. We hypothesize that volatile sublimation, possibly of water ice, sustains activity near perihelion.

papers.title: mm-jets in the multi-messenger era
papers.abstract: Jets and outflows operate across the full cosmic mass scale from young stellar objects (YSOs) and X-ray binaries (XRBs) to active galactic nuclei (AGN), gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), and tidal disruption events (TDEs), shaping many time-domain and multi-messenger transients. Key questions concern on how jets are launched, accelerated and collimated; where and how they dissipate energy and accelerate particles; and how they couple to their environments to set electromagnetic counterpart diversity and feedback. Millimeter and sub-millimeter observations uniquely address these questions by tracking the evolving synchrotron turnover for robust calorimetry and Lorentz-factor constraints, providing full-Stokes polarization and Faraday diagnostics close to the jet base, and enabling high-resolution imaging from Galactic ejecta to event-horizon-scale AGN jet bases via global Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI). We describe the jet and outflow science enabled by ALMA2040, a next-generation mm/sub-mm interferometer combining an order-of-magnitude sensitivity gain with rapid-response observing, simultaneous multi-band coverage, full-Stokes polarimetry, and integration with global VLBI networks. These capabilities will enable statistically controlled, trigger-driven samples spanning XRB outbursts, early GRB afterglows, protostellar disk winds and jet launching, AGN jet bases, and jetted TDEs, establishing mm/sub-mm astronomy as a cornerstone of time-domain and multi-messenger jet physics in the 2040s and beyond.

papers.title: Optimal Strategies for Gravitational-Wave Memory Detection with Noise Marginalization in Pulsar Timing Arrays
papers.abstract: Current pulsar timing arrays could detect gravitational wave memory, which would provide a unique test of general relativity. In order to optimize our searches for gravitational wave memory in pulsar timing arrays, we integrate the optimal frequentist statistics for GW memory into the \texttt{enterprise} code suite. We additionally test a noise marginalized version of this statistic, and compare it's effectiveness to the simpler maximum posterior method. We perform these tests on simulated pulsar timing array with red and white noise content, as well as the NANOGrav $15$-year data set. We find no significant variations in our detection statistics between the noise-marginalized and the maximum-posterior methods for the simulated datasets, and only small variations in the NANOGrav $15$-year comparisons. We conclude that for realistic PTAs the noise-marginalization method could be useful for assigning a false alarm probability to Bayesian results, though the maximum posterior method is sufficient for identifying potentially detectable signals.

papers.title: Study of pulse jitter characteristics of PSR J1744-1134: Towards high precision pulsar timing with InPTA
papers.abstract: Variations in the shapes of individual pulses introduce a broadband noise component in pulsar times of arrival beyond what is expected from radiometer noise, referred to as the jitter noise. This noise limits the timing accuracy and, consequently, the sensitivity required for the detection of nanohertz gravitational waves using pulsar timing arrays. Accurate characterization of jitter noise, including its amplitude and frequency dependence, is therefore essential for each pulsar. In this work, we present the first detailed study of jitter noise in PSR J1744-1134 over the frequency range 300-500 MHz, using observations from the Indian Pulsar Timing Array experiment conducted with the upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope. We detect clear signatures of jitter in this pulsar through pulse-level analysis and Bayesian inference. Furthermore, we investigated the frequency dependence of the jitter noise and compared our results with earlier measurements at higher frequencies. The observed differences in jitter amplitude suggest a possible frequency evolution, highlighting the importance of low-frequency studies for improving pulsar timing precision and accuracy. We also investigated the effect of jitter on the high precision dispersion measure derived from our observations and found that jitter is not the limiting factor for DM precision achieved for this pulsar in the given observation timescale.

papers.title: Displacement-noise-free gravitational-wave detector using quantum tomography of photon orbital angular momentum states
papers.abstract: Gravitational waves (GWs) induce quantum transitions between photon orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) states with amplitudes $\alpha_{\pm}$. Exploiting this effect, we present a displacement-noise-free detection framework that extracts GW information from the OAM Hilbert space. Parametrized quantum state tomography of the GW-induced OAM sidebands enables a single V-shaped detector to resolve all seven wave parameters: the frequency, propagation direction, two polarization amplitudes, and initial phase of each polarization. Direct detection of the sidebands yields a weak signal of approximately $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{W}$. We therefore introduce a stronger reference state $r |0>_{\mathrm{P}}$, with $r=0.01$, to enhance the detected signal. For an arm length of $L=4\,\mathrm{m}$, $N=160$ round trips, a paraxial parameter of $\gamma=0.1$, an incident light power of $P_{\mathrm{BS}}=10\,\mathrm{kW}$, a wavelength of $\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}=1064\,\mathrm{nm}$, and GW amplitudes of $A=10^{-18}$, we estimate sideband transition amplitudes of $|\alpha_{\pm}|\sim10^{-10}$ and signal powers of order $1\,\mathrm{nW}$, scaling as $P_{\mathrm{BS}}\alpha_{\pm}\propto P_{\mathrm{BS}}ANL\gamma/\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}$. The shot-noise-limited sensitivity floor is $S^{1/2}_n=1.6\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{Hz}^{-1/2}$. Because the scheme measures OAM transition amplitudes rather than differential arm lengths, it is intrinsically free from displacement noise and provides a broadband probe of GWs, specifically bridging the $0.1$--$10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ mid-frequency gap.

papers.title: Dark Matter Particle Explorer: Ten-Year On-Orbit Performance and Scientific Outcomes
papers.abstract: The Dark Matter Particle Explorer (DAMPE, also known as ``Wukong'') is the first scientific space mission within the framework of the Strategic Pioneer Program on Space Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The main scientific objectives of DAMPE include indirect detection of dark matter, cosmic-ray physics, and high energy gamma-ray astronomy. Thanks to its large geometrical factor and thick imaging calorimeter, DAMPE could effectively detect cosmic-ray electrons (including positrons) and gamma-rays up to 10~TeV, and nuclei up to PeV. Since launched on 17 December 2015 into a Sun-synchronous orbit, DAMPE has been smoothly operating on orbit for more than ten years. Here we present an overview of instrument, on-orbit status, and highlight scientific results of DAMPE, including the measurements of the all-electron energy spectrum and the spectra of protons and other nuclei, and high energy gamma-ray line search.

papers.title: A machine-learning-driven dataset of 144,111 polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon infrared spectra for interpreting aromatic infrared bands
papers.abstract: The interpretation of interstellar aromatic infrared bands (AIBs) relies on reference spectral libraries, but the chemical space covered by existing databases remains incomplete relative to the vast structural diversity of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) expected in the interstellar medium. We present a large-scale, high-throughput PAH infrared (IR) spectral database that complements existing reference libraries by providing significantly more continuous coverage of the PAH chemical space for small to medium-sized PAHs. We used a machine-learning double-harmonic (ML-DH) framework that integrates neural network force fields with electronic dipole models. This framework achieves quantum-chemical accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. It has been validated against independent density functional theory calculations and benchmark spectral databases. The resulting dataset comprises 144,111 IR spectra for 48,037 closed-shell, even-carbon benzenoid PAH structures across neutral, cationic, and anionic charge states, complete with per-spectrum uncertainty estimates. The spectral library, optimized geometries, and model code are publicly available. They can be used to complement existing libraries for interpreting and modeling JWST AIB observations and those from future IR missions.

papers.title: Polarization Properties of Thomson-Scattering Triaxial Ellipsoids
papers.abstract: Polarimetry is a powerful tool for constraining the geometry of distant astrophysical objects. Continuum polarization induced by Thomson scattering can probe the photospheric geometry of transients and provide insight into their explosion mechanisms. We systematically study continuum polarization from spheroids over a broader range of deformations and viewing angles than considered previously, and generalize the calculation to triaxial ellipsoids. We find that strongly deformed spheroids exhibit a non-monotonic dependence of polarization on viewing angle, a behavior overlooked in previous studies. Triaxial ellipsoids show more diverse polarization signatures, but their qualitative behavior can be understood from the area of surface elements viewed nearly edge-on, where the local polarization is strongest. Our results provide a simple physical understanding of the dependence of polarization on photospheric geometry and help constrain the geometry of astrophysical transients through polarimetric observations. The computational results of this study will be made publicly available for use in future research.

papers.title: Time-reversible timestepping in many-body planetary systems
papers.abstract: Simulating chaotic planetary system evolution requires resolving small time-scales due to close encounters, scattering, collisions, and more. Simulations typically assign fixed timesteps to all particles, however, which is inefficient and wastes compute resources in a chaotically evolving system; moreover, it may under-resolve the simulation. Hybrid methods are a blunt tool for resolving small time-scales as they do not allow for fine-grained adaptation. Assigning individual timesteps, which vary in time, to planetary bodies usually violates desirable properties such as symplecticity and reversibility. In this work, we develop an "almost" exactly time-reversible direct $N$-body integrator, MTR, in which each pair of planets gets its own timestep, which itself can vary as the system evolves. In contrast to our previous work, we achieve this adaptation on the fly, independent of a global timestep. We provide a C version of the code and test it on several problems, demonstrating no energy error drift, as expected of a reversible method. At large particle numbers, up to $N = 975$, we compare against the state-of-the-art GPLUM code, which we can use in direct Hermite mode (for which it is not optimized) or tree mode (for which it is). MTR provides a speedup of up to two orders of magnitude compared to the Hermite mode, while agreeing with the distribution of orbits. In our default configuration, MTR's speed matches or improves on the tree mode's speed, by up to an order magnitude, despite the tree mode's faster and approximate force calculation.

papers.title: Identifying deformed exoplanets with JWST and Ariel: A target selection metric for phase curve observations
papers.abstract: The shape of an exoplanet encodes fundamental information about its internal structure. For close-in giant planets, strong stellar tidal forces induce measurable deformations that can be probed through high-precision photometry. These deformations are quantified by the fluid Love numbers, which characterise a planet's response to external perturbations and are directly linked to its internal density distribution. In this work, we assess the potential of JWST and the future Ariel mission to constrain the Love numbers of hot Jupiters through full-orbit phase curve observations. To identify the most promising targets for this science case, we introduce a new detection metric, the deformation metric (D), which combines the expected deformation amplitude with the anticipated photometric signal-to-noise ratio. We apply this metric to the Ariel target list and identify WASP-33 b, WASP-76 b, and HAT-P-32 b as the three most favourable targets that currently lack Love number measurements. Using WASP-76 b as a benchmark case, we perform end-to-end retrieval simulations and show that a single continuous JWST phase curve observation can constrain the Love number $h_{2f}$ to a precision of $\sigma_{h_2f} \approx 0.09$, while a single Ariel visit could achieve $\sigma_{h_{2f}} \approx 0.18$. Such precision is likely sufficient for Love number measurements to provide meaningful constraints on planetary interior models and to distinguish between competing interior-structure scenarios, opening a new observational avenue for probing the deep interiors of exoplanets.

papers.title: Singles in Disguise: Kepler's Low-SNR Single-Transiting Systems as Incompletely Detected Multis
papers.abstract: NASA's Kepler mission found more systems with one transiting planet (``singles'') than expected from those with several (``multis''). This excess was first taken as evidence for a Kepler dichotomy -- a second population of intrinsically single or highly inclined systems -- but later work argued that selection effects acting on a single population can reproduce it. Singles also show a puzzling excess of low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) detections relative to multis. The question arises whether this excess reflects false positives, a selection effect, or an inherent population difference. Here we show, using the ExoMOD population synthesis model and the Kepler DR25 catalog, that multis drawn from the same parent population as singles have shorter mean orbital periods, and thus higher-SNR detections on average. Detecting several planets in one system favors compact architectures, so long-period, low-SNR detections are preferentially cataloged as singles, most of them intrinsically multi-planet systems whose other planets went undetected. The low-SNR excess of singles therefore requires neither false positives nor a Kepler dichotomy but rather only the geometry and period sensitivity of transit detection.

papers.title: JWST Observations of RR Lyrae in Leo P
papers.abstract: We analyze co-spatial HST/ACS and JWST/NIRCam time-series photometric observations of RR Lyrae in the low-metallicity dwarf galaxy Leo P. This study provides a new opportunity to explore the properties of and potential for metal-poor RR Lyrae studies with JWST using well-understood relationships from past HST work. We identify 20 RR Lyrae in the HST imaging and 15 RR Lyrae in the JWST imaging. We determine the periods, amplitudes, and mean magnitudes for each of the RR Lyrae. We fit the Period-Wesenheit-Metallicity (PWZ) function to the HST RR Lyrae population, and obtain a Gaia-consistent RR Lyrae-based distance to Leo P of $\mu = 26.04\pm0.07$ ($1.61\pm0.06$ Mpc), consistent with existing distance measurements. We determine a JWST-based PWZ using Leo P data along with previous JWST RR Lyrae observations in WLM. The simultaneous fit decreases the mean fractional uncertainty by 31% on the slope and by 11% on the intercept, increasing the constraining power as compared to the existing calibration.

papers.title: A Sample of Thick-Disk Stars Hosting Hot Jupiters
papers.abstract: We present a homogeneous analysis of 268 confirmed and candidate transiting hot-Jupiter host stars with 4800K < Teff < 6200K. We combine high-resolution TRES spectra, Gaia, 2MASS and WISE photometry, and Gaia astrometry to determine these stars' Teff, log g, Rstar, [alpha/Fe] and [Fe/H]. Based on their [alpha/Fe] and [Fe/H], we classify the stars as members of the Milky Way's low-[alpha/Fe] thin disk, high-[alpha/Fe] thick disk or an ambiguous intermediate population. We identify two confirmed hot Jupiters (WASP-81 b and TOI-5322 b) and three candidate hot Jupiters (TOI-3118.01, TOI-2728.01, and TOI-5781.01) as orbiting previously-unrecognized members of the high-alpha thick disk. We compare the properties of the confirmed planets in the three populations and note two indications of a potential difference between the populations: both high-[alpha/Fe] confirmed planets and eight out of the eleven ambiguous-disk confirmed planets are less massive than the median low-[alpha/Fe] planet, and none of our high-[alpha/Fe] or ambiguous confirmed planets have orbital periods shorter than 2.7 d, when 22% of our low-[alpha/Fe] population do. These differences may reflect variations in giant-planet formation across galactic environments, evolutionary effects, or differing stellar properties between the high- and low-[alpha/Fe] populations. Our catalog is the largest sample of chemically-identified high-[alpha/Fe] thick-disk confirmed and candidate hot-Jupiter host stars. These ancient systems, with ages > 8 Gyr, may allow for a better understanding of how the formation of hot Jupiters depends on galactic environment, and how their orbits evolve over very long time scales.
